title: Counting — and what happens to the noun
goal: Count from zero to a million, give your age, phone number, and prices — while setting up the rule that trips up nearly every learner: the noun changes form three ways depending on the number in front of it.
bekal: say the numbers 0-1,000 and answer *Koliko imate godina?*
form the plural of masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns
choose the right noun form after 1, after 2-4, and after 5 and up

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Upis na kurs
dialogs.intro: Budi signs up for a Bosnian course at a small school near Ferhadija. The clerk uses *Vi* from start to finish — watch the verb forms.

lines.speaker: Referentica:
lines.id: Good afternoon! What is your name?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nula šest dva — tri četiri pet — sedam osam devet.
lines.id: Zero six two, three four five, seven eight nine.
lines.literal: zero six two — three four five — seven eight nine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ulica Ferhadija, broj sedamnaest, drugi sprat.
lines.id: Ferhadija Street, number seventeen, second floor.
lines.literal: street Ferhadija, number seventeen, second-m floor.

lines.speaker: Referentica:
lines.text: Koliko dugo ste već u Sarajevu?
lines.id: How long have you been in Sarajevo?
lines.literal: how-much long you(pl)-are already in Sarajevo-loc?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tri mjeseca. Došao sam u junu.
lines.id: Three months. I came in June.
lines.literal: three months-gen. come-m I-am in June-loc.

lines.speaker: Referentica:
lines.text: Kurs ima dvadeset časova i košta dvjesto maraka.
lines.id: The course is twenty lessons and costs two hundred marks.
lines.literal: course it-has twenty hours-gen-pl and it-costs two-hundred marks-gen-pl.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: U redu. Koliko studenata ima u grupi?
lines.id: All right. How many students are in a class?
lines.literal: in order. how-many students-gen-pl it-has in group-loc?

lines.speaker: Referentica:
lines.text: Osam — pet žena i tri muškarca. Počinjemo u ponedjeljak.
lines.id: Eight — five women and three men. We start on Monday.
lines.literal: eight — five women-gen-pl and three men-gen. we-start on Monday-acc.

notes: **Notice the noun endings change three ways in this dialogue:** *tri mjeseca* (after 2-4), *dvadeset časova* and *pet žena* (after 5 and up), *drugi sprat* (after an ordinal, the normal form). That is the grammar of this unit, and it works exactly the same for every noun in Bosnian.

***Koliko imate godina?* — age counts as something you have.** Literally "how many years do you have?" The answer must use *godina*: *Imam dvadeset osam godina.* Answering with just the number sounds unfinished.

**Phone numbers are read digit by digit, in groups of three.** If there's a double digit, Bosnians sometimes say *dva puta pet* ("two times five") for 55. *Nula* is zero; don't use the letter O the way English speakers often do.

**Bosnian currency: *konvertibilna marka*, written KM or BAM.** One mark = a hundred *feninga*. The name comes from the German mark, and its value is pegged to the euro (€1 ≈ 1.96 KM) — so a rough rule: halve it to get euros. In conversation people say *maraka* or just *KM* (said *ka-em*).

**Floors are counted the European way.** *Prizemlje* is the ground floor, *prvi sprat* is the floor above it — what Americans call the second floor. So Budi's *drugi sprat* is the third floor in American terms. This misunderstanding causes more late arrivals than it should.

grammars.title: Brojevi — numbers from zero to a million
body: The system is regular and almost free of surprises. Once you know one to ten, you can build the rest yourself.
after: **Eleven to nineteen: the number stem + *-naest*.** *Jedan → jedanaest*, *pet → petnaest*, *devet → devetnaest*. Two are slightly shortened: *četiri → četrnaest*, *šest → šesnaest*. Stress goes near the front: yeh-dah-NAH-ehst sounds wrong; the right way is *yeh-DAH-nah-ehst*.

**Tens: the number stem + *-deset*.** *Tri → trideset*, *pet → pedeset*, *sedam → sedamdeset*. Two change their sound: *četiri → četrdeset*, *šest → šezdeset*. Compound numbers are simply strung together: *dvadeset jedan* (21), *četrdeset pet* (45), *devedeset devet* (99) — no "and" in the middle, unlike German or Dutch.

**Only *jedan* and *dva* have gender.** *Jedan grad, jedna kafa, jedno pivo.* And the one people miss most: **dva** for masculine and neuter words, **dvije** for feminine words. *Dva brata* but *dvije sestre*; *dva piva* but *dvije kafe*. Numbers from three up never change.

**Ordinals are formed like adjectives**, so their endings follow the noun: *prvi* (first), *drugi* (second), *treći*, *četvrti*, *peti*, *šesti*, *sedmi*, *osmi*, *deveti*, *deseti*. *Prvi sprat, prva soba, prvo pitanje.* Note that *drugi* has a second meaning: "other" — *drugi grad* can mean "the second city" or "another city", and context decides.

grammars.title: Nouns after numbers — three forms, not one
body: This is the rule that most often makes learners stop mid-sentence. The good news: it has only three lines, and it applies the same way to every noun without exception.
after: **What decides is the last digit.** *Dvadeset jedna godina* (21 years) goes back to the singular because it ends in 1. *Trideset tri godine* uses the 2-4 form. *Dvadeset pet godina* uses the genitive plural. The only exception: **11 to 14 always take the genitive plural** even though they end in 1-4 — *jedanaest godina*, *četrnaest godina*.

**Why a separate form for 2-4?** Because early Slavic had a special form for "exactly two", and its remains froze around 2, 3, and 4. There's no point hunting for the logic now — all you need is to drill three examples until they come out by themselves: *jedna kafa, dvije kafe, pet kafa*.

**You already have half the genitive endings.** Genitive singular: masculine and neuter add **-a** (*grad → grada*, *pivo → piva*), feminine changes to **-e** (*godina → godine*). Genitive plural: masculine adds **-ova / -eva** (*gradovi → gradova*), while feminine and neuter have **no ending at all** (*godine → godina*, *piva → piva*). The whole story is in unit 8.

**The verb follows too.** After 1 it is singular (*jedan student je ovdje*), after 2-4 plural (*dva studenta su ovdje*), after 5 and up it is **neuter singular**: *Pet studenata je ovdje.* It sounds strange, but that's how it is — and hardly any foreign speaker notices.

blocks.text: The plural is formed with an ending, and the ending is set by the word's gender — so three patterns, one per gender. Once again, proof of why you need to note the gender from the very first word.

blocks.text: One-syllable masculine words insert *-ov-* (or *-ev-* after *č, ć, š, ž, đ, dž, j, lj, nj*) before the ending. *Grad → gradovi*, *sat → satovi*, *voz → vozovi*, but *nož → noževi*, *muž → muževi*. Words of two or more syllables don't need it: *prozor → prozori*, *student → studenti*.

blocks.title: Five plurals to learn separately
items: *čovjek* (person) → **ljudi** — a completely different word, just like *person / people*. *Ljudi su dobri.*
*brat* (brother) → **braća**, also feminine singular: *moja braća su ovdje*.
*sat* has two plurals with different meanings: **sati** = hours (units of time), **satovi** = clocks/watches. *Tri sata* = three hours; *tri satova* = three clocks.

blocks.text: One question word opens almost every question with a number in it: *koliko* (how much / how many). It is always followed by the genitive plural, just like the big numbers.

blocks.text: Bosnian money: the **konvertibilna marka** (KM), a hundred *feninga*. Denominations in circulation: 1, 2, 5 KM as coins; 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 KM as notes. For prices with change, people say the marks first: *tri marke i pedeset* (3.50 KM), often shortened to *tri i po* — "three and a half".

One small trap that often comes up at the till: **marka itself is feminine**, so *jedna marka, dvije marke, pet maraka*. If you say *dva marke*, everyone will still understand, but *dvije marke* is correct. And in Bosnia prices are written with a comma for the decimals — *3,50 KM*, not *3.50*.

answers: Imam dvadeset osam godina. — Koliko košta? Pet maraka. — Imam dvije sestre. — Kurs ima dvadeset časova. — U grupi ima osam ljudi. — Živim ovdje tri mjeseca.
